hypothesis.title: Lipschitz-Constrained EEGNet for Robust and Interpretable BCI Classification
hypothesis.summary: This paper proposes a Lipschitz-constrained variant of EEGNet (LC-EEGNet) that enforces smoothness in feature transformations to improve robustness against adversarial perturbations while maintaining classification accuracy. By integrating Parseval tight frame constraints into EEGNet's convolutional layers, the model limits the Lipschitz constant of its transformations, reducing sensitivity to small input variations. We validate this approach on P300, ERN, MRCP, and SMR datasets with both clean and adversarially perturbed inputs, comparing against standard EEGNet and adversarially trained baselines.
hypothesis.gap: Existing EEGNet architectures lack formal robustness guarantees against adversarial attacks, which is critical for safety-critical BCI applications. Current robustness methods like adversarial training are data-intensive and not tailored to EEG's temporal-spatial characteristics.
hypothesis.approach: We modify EEGNet by constraining weight matrices in temporal and spatial convolutional layers to be approximate Parseval tight frames, ensuring bounded Lipschitz constants. This is enforced via spectral normalization during training without additional adversarial examples. We preserve EEGNet's interpretability through visualization techniques adapted to the constrained layers.
hypothesis.evaluation: We compare LC-EEGNet against standard EEGNet, adversarially trained EEGNet, and FBCSP on four BCI paradigms using clean data and three adversarial attack types (FGSM, PGD, CLEVER-based). Metrics include classification accuracy, Lipschitz constant estimates, and CLEVER scores for robustness certification.

refined.title: Lipschitz-Constrained EEGNet for Adversarially Robust BCI Classification
refined.summary: This paper introduces LC-EEGNet, a variant of EEGNet that enforces bounded Lipschitz constants via Parseval tight frame constraints on convolutional layers. By limiting the model's sensitivity to input perturbations, LC-EEGNet aims to improve robustness against adversarial attacks while maintaining classification accuracy. We evaluate LC-EEGNet on four BCI paradigms (P300, ERN, MRCP, SMR) under clean and adversarial conditions, comparing it to standard EEGNet and adversarially trained baselines.
refined.gap: While ref-021 demonstrates adversarial detection for EEG-based BCIs, no work has integrated formal Lipschitz constraints into EEGNet to provide provable robustness guarantees. Existing adversarial training methods (e.g., ref-024) are data-intensive and do not explicitly bound the model's sensitivity to input perturbations.
refined.approach: LC-EEGNet modifies EEGNet's temporal and spatial convolutional layers by constraining weight matrices to approximate Parseval tight frames, ensuring a Lipschitz constant ≤1. This is enforced via spectral normalization during training, without adversarial examples. The model's architecture and interpretability techniques (ref-001) remain unchanged except for the constrained layers. The core difference from ref-010 is the application of Parseval constraints to EEG-specific convolutional structures.
refined.evaluation: We compare LC-EEGNet with standard EEGNet and adversarially trained EEGNet on four BCI datasets (ref-001) under clean inputs and three white-box attacks (FGSM, PGD with ε=0.1, 20 steps). Metrics include classification accuracy, Lipschitz constant estimates (computed via ref-020's SDP method), and CLEVER scores (ref-009). An ablation study isolates the effect of Parseval constraints by comparing against spectral normalization alone (ref-010).

refined.title: Parseval EEGNet: Lipschitz-Constrained EEG Classification with Formal Robustness Guarantees
refined.summary: This paper introduces Parseval EEGNet, an EEGNet variant with Parseval tight frame constraints on convolutional layers to bound the network's Lipschitz constant. This constraint limits the network's sensitivity to input perturbations while preserving classification accuracy. The approach is evaluated on P300, ERN, MRCP, and SMR datasets from MOABB, comparing clean/perturbed accuracy and attack success rates against standard EEGNet and adversarially trained baselines under FGSM/PGD attacks.
refined.gap: While EEGNet [ref-001] generalizes across BCI paradigms, it lacks formal robustness guarantees. Ref-010 shows Lipschitz-constrained networks (Parseval networks) provide formal robustness bounds, but this has not been applied to EEG. The gap is the absence of a method to provide provable perturbation bounds for EEG-based BCIs, which is necessary for safety-critical applications where input noise or adversarial attacks could cause misclassification.
refined.approach: Parseval EEGNet replaces standard convolutional layers in EEGNet with Parseval tight frame-constrained layers, ensuring the Lipschitz constant of each layer is ≤1. The input is raw EEG time-series, and the output is class probabilities. The core difference from [ref-001] is the use of orthogonalized weight matrices in depthwise and separable convolutions, maintained via projection during SGD. The objective is cross-entropy loss, with an additional constraint on weight matrices to remain approximately Parseval. No adversarial training is used, isolating the effect of Lipschitz constraints.
refined.evaluation: Evaluate on four BCI paradigms (P300, ERN, MRCP, SMR) from MOABB [ref-007] using the same datasets as [ref-001]. Baselines: standard EEGNet [ref-001] and adversarially trained EEGNet. Metrics: (1) clean test accuracy, (2) perturbed test accuracy under FGSM (ε=0.1) and PGD (10 steps, ε=0.01/step), (3) attack success rate. Ablation: compare Parseval EEGNet with/without Lipschitz constraints to isolate the effect of the proposed method. All experiments use white-box attacks, as in [ref-021].

hypothesis.title: Cross-Paradigm EEG Feature Generalization via Meta-Learned Initialization
hypothesis.summary: We hypothesize that meta-learning can enable EEGNet to generalize across BCI paradigms with minimal task-specific data by learning paradigm-agnostic feature extraction patterns. Our approach uses Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) to initialize EEGNet weights on multiple paradigms, allowing fast adaptation to new tasks. We evaluate this on leave-one-paradigm-out scenarios, measuring adaptation speed and final accuracy against standard EEGNet and MOABB benchmark methods.
hypothesis.gap: While EEGNet shows cross-paradigm generalization, its performance degrades with limited target paradigm data. Existing approaches require paradigm-specific hyperparameter tuning or extensive retraining, limiting practical BCI deployment.
hypothesis.approach: We implement MAML training for EEGNet across P300, ERN, MRCP, and SMR datasets, optimizing for fast adaptation to new subjects/paradigms. The meta-initialization captures common EEG feature patterns (e.g., temporal filtering, spatial patterns) while allowing task-specific fine-tuning. We analyze learned features to identify paradigm-invariant vs. paradigm-specific components.
hypothesis.evaluation: We compare meta-EEGNet against standard EEGNet, FBCSP, and shallow CNNs in few-shot learning scenarios (1-10 training trials). Metrics include adaptation accuracy, convergence speed, and feature similarity across paradigms using centered kernel alignment.
